content: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review aimed at evaluating the benefits and adverse effects of vaccines in preventing infections among adults with haematological malignancies. Cancer is a major cause of mortality in high-income countries, with nearly 10 million deaths globally in 2020, according to the World Health Organization. Haematological malignancies, which rank among the 10 most common cancer types in high-income countries, originate from the myeloid or lymphatic systems and can affect the peripheral blood, bone marrow, or lymph nodes, with potential involvement of other organs. Lymphoid cancers include non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute and chronic leukaemia, and multiple myeloma. Myeloid cancers encompass conditions such as acute and chronic myeloid leukaemia, polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, primary myelofibrosis, mastocytosis, and myelodysplastic syndromes. Individuals with haematological malignancies are at an elevated risk of infections due to their underlying disease or the immunosuppressive therapies they undergo. Approximately 60% of cancer-related deaths are either directly caused by or associated with infections. Compared to patients with solid tumours, those with haematological malignancies experience higher levels of immunosuppression, as the neoplastic processes compromise the immune system, and treatments often result in prolonged neutropenia. The degree of vulnerability to infections depends on the type of immune deficiency (e.g., T-cell versus B-cell), the stage and clinical status of the malignancy, and the duration and intensity of therapy. While survival rates have improved with the advent of antineoplastic agents, particularly targeted therapies, these treatments impair both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, thereby increasing the risk of infections. Anti-infective therapies, such as antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals, can interfere with anticancer treatments, reducing their efficacy and increasing toxicity. This often necessitates delaying either anticancer or anti-infective therapies, which can compromise patient outcomes. Vaccination offers a preventive strategy against certain infections, such as influenza, SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal disease, and meningococcal disease. Vaccines are categorized based on the pathogens used in their development. Conventional vaccines include live-attenuated pathogens (e.g., measles, mumps, rubella), inactivated pathogens (e.g., polio, early influenza vaccines), and conjugate vaccines (e.g., human papillomavirus, hepatitis B). Novel vaccine technologies, such as nucleic acid vaccines and vector-based vaccines, leverage genome sequencing. For instance, mRNA vaccines (e.g., BNT162b2, mRNA-1273) use engineered mRNA to instruct cells to produce the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, prompting the immune system to generate protective antibodies. Vector-based vaccines (e.g., AZD1222, AD26.COV2.S) use a modified virus to deliver genetic material from the target pathogen, enabling the immune system to produce a defensive response. Live-attenuated vaccines, which mimic natural infections, elicit robust cellular and humoral immune responses in healthy individuals but are contraindicated in immunocompromised patients due to the risk of severe disease. However, in certain cases, such as patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia under observation or those in remission from acute myeloid leukaemia, live-attenuated vaccines like the MMR vaccine may be considered before initiating immunosuppressive therapy. Inactivated and conjugate vaccines, while less immunogenic, can still elicit protective immune responses, often requiring booster doses. Despite reduced immune responses to vaccines in individuals with haematological malignancies compared to healthy individuals, vaccination can still prevent or mitigate the severity of infections, reduce hospitalizations, and lower infection-related mortality. However, current national and international guidelines on vaccination for this patient population are inconsistent. For example, the European Conference on Infections in Leukaemia recommends revaccination for cancer patients post-stem cell transplantation but provides limited guidance for those not undergoing transplantation. Similarly, the Infectious Diseases Society of America advises vaccination with inactivated vaccines and live varicella and MMR vaccines three months after chemotherapy, with additional delays for patients treated with anti-B-cell antibodies. The Canadian Immunization Guide recommends vaccinating individuals with haematological malignancies using inactivated vaccines at least two weeks before starting immunosuppressive therapy or during periods of minimal immunosuppression, except in cases of high infection risk. Pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide vaccines, as well as a single dose of Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine, are recommended for this population. Vaccination is contraindicated in individuals with severe neutropenia (neutrophil counts < 500/µL) to avoid febrile episodes. COVID-19 has been shown to have worse outcomes in patients with haematological malignancies, with significantly higher mortality rates, underscoring the need to prioritize vaccination for these individuals. Despite the importance of vaccination, it is rarely and inconsistently addressed in disease-specific guidelines or evidence-based supportive care recommendations. The German Society for Hematology and Medical Oncology has identified the prevention of infections in cancer patients as a critical research area, emphasizing the need for better understanding of vaccine efficacy and clinical outcomes in this population. Current research often focuses on laboratory outcomes, such as antibody levels and T-cell responses, which do not always correlate with patient-relevant clinical outcomes. There is an urgent need to evaluate the impact of vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, on clinical outcomes in patients with haematological malignancies. This review will focus on patient-relevant outcomes, identified through consultations with patients and their representatives, and will exclude laboratory outcomes. It will specifically address adults with haematological malignancies who are not undergoing cellular therapies. This review is part of a broader series, with other reviews focusing on individuals with solid tumours and those receiving cellular therapies, such as stem cell transplantation or CAR-T cell therapy.
